name: Part 3 — Discussion
tagline: Four minutes of abstract questions, and an examiner who will push back
blurb: Part 3 separates candidates more sharply than any other part, because it is the only one that assesses reasoning rather than recall. It is also the part most damaged by preparation, since memorised opinions cannot survive a follow-up question.

facts: 4 to 5 minutes, thematically linked to the Part 2 topic but progressively more abstract.
Comparison, cause, opinion, speculation about the future, and evaluation of a proposal.
The examiner may ask Why do you think that? or offer a counter-position. This is probing built into the test, not disagreement.
The examiner may cut you off to fit the remaining questions. Again, timing, not judgement.
There are no marks for facts, statistics or being right. The marks are for how you reason, in English.
brief.what: Two descriptor phrases govern this part. Band 7 asks for flexible use of discourse markers, connectives and cohesive features — meaning markers that do different jobs, not four repetitions of moreover. Band 8 asks that topics be developed coherently and appropriately, and that hesitation be content related rather than to find words. Taken together: the examiner wants to hear you think, in real time, in structured English. Answers that arrive pre-formed and unvarying score lower than answers that visibly reason, even slightly imperfect ones.
myths: Invented statistics are a liability and real ones are not credited. What is credited is a clear claim with a reason that holds.
A firmly argued one-sided answer can reach Band 8 if the reasoning is sharp. Half-argued balance reads as indecision and often produces self-contradiction.
“Saying ‘I've never thought about that’ loses marks.”
Said and then followed by visible thinking aloud, it is entirely band-compatible and sounds far more credible than an instant rehearsed opinion.
The examiner has no position. Push-back is a prompt to extend, and extending is exactly what it is testing.

tactics.name: Reframe the contested term
tactics.why: Most Part 3 questions contain one word doing all the work — too much, important, better, successful. Defining it before answering is the clearest single marker of Band 8 reasoning.
tactics.do: Do people depend too much on technology? → It hinges on what we mean by 'too much', because dependence and over-dependence get lumped together far too casually.
tactics.dont: Answering the surface question and hoping the reasoning shows up later.

band.b7: Notes that the answer depends on how the term is understood.
band.b8: Separates two senses of the term and shows that they call for opposite answers.

tactics.name: Concede, then rebut
tactics.why: Granting the opposing view before answering it demonstrates that you have considered it, which is what the examiner cannot otherwise observe.
tactics.do: There is some truth in that — screen time has obviously gone up. But the figure on its own tells you nothing about what the screen is being used for.
tactics.dont: No, I disagree. Flat contradiction gives the examiner nothing to rate.

band.b7: Concedes a specific point, then rebuts it.
band.b8: Concedes the strongest version of the opposing point, which makes the rebuttal worth more.

tactics.name: Categorise
tactics.why: Sorting a general question into cases is visible reasoning, and it also solves the problem of having nothing more to say.
tactics.do: Four reliable axes: by age group, by sector, by degree, and by reversibility. It depends whether the decision can be undone. For reversible ones, decide fast and alone. For irreversible ones, consult.

band.b7: Divides the question into two cases and treats each.
band.b8: Names the principle that decides which case applies.

tactics.name: Supply your own counter-example
tactics.why: Textbook examples are recognisable and weightless. An example you constructed shows the reasoning is live.
tactics.do: A surgeon relying on imaging isn't dependent in any troubling sense; she's specialised. A teenager who can't sleep without a phone is something else entirely.
tactics.dont: For example, in some countries, people use technology a lot.

band.b7: Gives a specific example that supports the claim.
band.b8: Gives a paired example that discriminates between two cases.

tactics.name: Frame it as a trade-off
tactics.why: Abstract questions rarely have right answers, and treating them as though they do produces thin reasoning. Naming what is gained and what is lost is more sophisticated and easier to sustain.
tactics.do: You gain access and lose attention. Whether that is worth it depends on what you were going to do with the attention.

band.b8: Identifies the condition under which the trade is worth making.

tactics.name: The conditional close
tactics.why: Ending on a condition rather than a verdict keeps the answer open, invites the follow-up, and delivers a complex structure at the same time.
tactics.do: Provided the fallbacks stay in place, I'd call it a reasonable trade rather than a problem.
tactics.dont: So in conclusion, it has both advantages and disadvantages. This is a written-essay ending and it sounds like one.

band.b8: Closes on a conditional forecast — what would have to be true for the answer to change.

tactics.name: Thinking aloud when you have no view
tactics.why: You will be asked something you have never considered. The recovery is not to invent an opinion but to narrate the process of forming one, which is precisely what fluency at this level looks like.
tactics.do: That's not something I've ever thought about, actually. My first instinct is that it would make no difference — though now that I say it out loud, I'm not sure that holds, because…
tactics.dont: Silence, or a rehearsed opinion visibly unrelated to the question.

band.b7: Admits uncertainty and reasons towards a position.
band.b8: Reasons towards a position and revises it mid-answer — which the descriptors credit, since the hesitation is content related.

lang.intro: Part 3 language is argumentative language, and the four functions that matter are conceding, distinguishing, speculating and generalising with a hedge. Precision matters more here than anywhere else in the test, which is why the softeners that work in Part 1 should be dropped.

items: there's some truth in that, but
The standard concession opener. Signals engagement rather than agreement.
A single word doing the whole job. Fronted, with a pause after it.
I'd accept that up to a point
Partial agreement with an implied limit — and the limit is what you say next.
Concedes a fact that weakens your own case, which paradoxically strengthens it.
that may well be the case, though
Formal concession. May well is stronger than may.
it hinges on what we mean by
The reframing move in one phrase. Reserve it for the question's key term.
there's a difference between X and Y
Plain and effective. The examiner is listening for the distinction, not the phrasing.
Two different things treated as one. Informal register inside a formal argument, which works well.
Reclassification in six words. That's not dependence, that's brittleness.
Politely sets aside a distraction and shows you noticed it.
Tentative prediction. More natural than I predict, which nobody says.
Marks an inference as following logically from what preceded.
Formal probability marker. One per answer; it is conspicuous.
Informal and honest, which suits speculation better than false confidence.
Attaches a condition to a forecast — the conditional close in miniature.
Broadly true with exceptions acknowledged. Safer than a bare generalisation.
Habitually true. Pairs naturally with a following exception.
More than half the time. Precise enough to be defensible.
The most useful hedging verb in the language. Banning devices outright tends to backfire.
Pre-empts the counter-example the examiner is about to raise.

phon.intro: In Part 3 pronunciation stops being about clarity and starts carrying argument. If the stress pattern does not mark the contrast, the reasoning does not land however well it is worded.

items.what: When you distinguish two things, English marks the distinction with stress. Said flat, dependence and over-dependence sounds like a repetition rather than a contrast, and the entire argument collapses.
items.drill: because dePENdence / and Over-dependence / get lumped toGEther far too CASually ↘ ‖ That's NOT dependence ↗ / that's BRITtleness ↘
items.note: Drill the contrasted pair ten times in isolation before attempting the sentence. If a listener cannot hear which of the two words is being emphasised, the distinction has not been made.

items.what: A concession rises; the rebuttal that follows falls. This pair of contours tells the listener that more is coming and that the second clause is the real claim — before either clause is understood.
items.drill: There's SOME truth in that ↗ / BUT the figure on its own ↗ / tells you NOthing about what the screen is USED for ↘
items.note: Candidates who fall on the concession sound as though they have agreed and then contradicted themselves.

items.what: The last strongly stressed word in a thought group signals what is new. Moving it changes what the sentence is about, and misplacing it makes an argument hard to follow even when every word is correct.
items.drill: It's not how much we LEAN on technology ↗ / it's whether there's anything to FALL BACK on ↘ / when it FAILS ↘
items.note: Say the same sentence three times, moving the emphasis each time, and notice how the meaning shifts. Control over this is what the Band 8 descriptor means by using stress to convey precise meaning.

drills.name: Single question, forty-five seconds
drills.set: One Part 3 question. No preparation. Forty-five seconds.
drills.aim: Calibrates length. Under thirty seconds is underdeveloped; over sixty invites interruption.

drills.name: The why chain
drills.set: One question, then answer Why? three times in succession.
drills.aim: Simulates examiner push-back. Most candidates run out of reasoning by the second why; the drill is designed to find that point and move it.

drills.name: Both sides, then choose
drills.set: One question. Ninety seconds: thirty for the case, thirty for the counter-case, thirty to decide and say why.
drills.aim: Builds the concede-rebut-verdict shape until it becomes the default.

drills.name: Reframe first
drills.set: Five questions. Rule: every answer must begin by defining a term in the question.
drills.aim: Makes the Band 8 opening move automatic rather than occasional.

check: fc
Each answer ran roughly thirty to forty-five seconds with development, not a single assertion.
fc
My discourse markers did different jobs — conceding, contrasting, attributing — rather than repeating.
fc
Pauses were spent choosing what to say, not hunting for a word.
lr
I used at least one concession phrase and one hedge.
lr
I avoided the Part 1 softeners — kind of, sort of — where precision was being assessed.
gr
At least one answer closed on a conditional.
gr
I used a complex structure that served the argument rather than decorated it.
pr
Contrasted terms were audibly stressed differently.
pr
Concession clauses rose and rebuttals fell.
x
I defined or qualified the key term in at least one answer.
x
I supplied at least one example of my own rather than a generic one.
x
When pushed with why, I extended rather than repeated.

strategies.intro: Part 3 questions look varied and are not. Six question types cover the entire discussion phase, and each has an answer shape that fits comfortably into the thirty to forty-five seconds the examiner is expecting. Knowing which type you have been asked is more than half the work.

groups.type: ADVANTAGES & DISADVANTAGES — What are the pros and cons of…?
groups.cue: Explicitly asks for both sides, or asks what are the benefits of…
groups.shape: Strongest advantage → Strongest disadvantage → Which outweighs which, and when
moves: Give one of each, developed, rather than three of each, listed. Listing is the default failure of this type.
The third move is compulsory. A balanced list with no verdict is a Band 6 answer however good the vocabulary.
Frame the verdict as a trade-off: what is gained, what is paid, and whether the trade is worth it.

ex.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of using social media?
ex.a: The obvious gain is reach… The cost, which people notice less, is that it flattens the difference between a friend and an acquaintance… On balance I'd say the trade is worth it for people who already have a social life offline, and actively harmful for people who don't.

groups.trap: Two lists and no conclusion. The descriptors reward development, and a verdict is what development leads to.

groups.cue: Asks for reasons behind a behaviour, usually other people's.
groups.shape: Most obvious reason, dispatched quickly → A less obvious reason, developed → Which one actually dominates
moves: Give the obvious reason in one clause and move past it. Examiners hear the obvious reason forty times a day.
The second reason is where the marks are. Look for a psychological, economic or generational explanation.
Ranking the two is the Band 8 move: the second is doing far more of the work than people assume.

ex.q: Why do some people find it difficult to make important decisions?
ex.a: Fear of being wrong, obviously. But I suspect the bigger factor is that we now have far more options than any previous generation… and choice overload paralyses people in a way that simple fear does not.

groups.trap: Three parallel reasons of equal weight. Parallel lists show vocabulary; ranked reasons show thinking.

groups.type: OPINION — Do you think…? / Do you agree that…?
moves: Commit. A clearly defended one-sided answer reaches Band 8; a fence-sitting answer rarely does.
Concede the strongest version of the opposing case, not a weak one. A weak concession is transparent.
Close on a condition rather than a restatement.

ex.q: Do you think people depend too much on technology?
ex.a: I'd say we do, though it depends on what counts as depending. There's a real case that this is just specialisation… but the difference is whether there's anything to fall back on… Provided the fallbacks stay in place, I'd call it a reasonable trade.

groups.trap: Answering both sides have merit and stopping. The examiner cannot rate a position that was never taken.

groups.cue: Two groups or two eras: young and old, city and countryside, now and the past.
groups.shape: Name the axis of difference → Each side on that axis → What explains the gap
moves: Name one axis and hold it. Comparing on four axes at once produces a list, not a comparison.
Give each side a sentence on the same axis so the contrast is audible.
Explain the gap. Description of a difference is Band 6; explanation of why it exists is Band 7 and above.

ex.q: Do young people and older people have different tastes in music?
ex.a: The real difference isn't genre, it's how they listen. My parents' generation bought albums and sat with them… Mine treats music as a background layer… and that's a consequence of streaming rather than of taste.

groups.trap: Stereotyping without hedging. Old people don't like modern music is both inaccurate and unhedged; as a rule, though there are obvious exceptions costs two seconds and buys credibility.

groups.type: PREDICTION — Will…? / Do you think … in the future?
groups.shape: Hedged prediction → Mechanism → What would falsify it
moves: Hedge properly: in all likelihood, my hunch is, if that trend holds. Flat certainty about the future sounds naive.
Give the mechanism, not just the outcome. It will increase is an assertion; it will increase because the cost has collapsed is an argument.
Naming what would make you wrong is a strong Band 8 move and takes one clause.

ex.q: Will technology become more reliable in the future?
ex.a: In all likelihood, yes, though not evenly. The mechanism is competitive: reliability is now a selling point… What would change my mind is if the pace of releases keeps outrunning the testing, which is roughly what's happening now.

groups.trap: Confident prophecy. Unhedged future claims read as unreflective and lose the modal range the question is offering.

groups.type: PROPOSAL — What should governments / schools / parents do?
groups.cue: Asks for a recommendation or solution.
groups.shape: One measure, specified → Why it works → Why the obvious alternative does not
moves: One measure, described concretely. Three vague measures score lower than one precise one.
Say by what mechanism it works. Raise awareness is not a mechanism.
Dismissing the obvious alternative shows you considered the field, which is otherwise invisible to the examiner.

ex.q: What should governments do to protect the environment?
ex.a: The measure I'd back is pricing — a genuine levy on single-use plastic at the point of sale. It works because it changes behaviour at the moment of the decision… Awareness campaigns fail precisely because they arrive weeks before the choice is made.

groups.trap: The government should raise awareness and make stricter laws. This sentence appears in thousands of Part 3 answers and contains no content.

extra.title: Handling the follow-up Why?
extra.html:
The examiner is trained to probe. When they ask why do you think that? they are not disagreeing — they are creating the opportunity to extend, which is what the band descriptors call development. Candidates who hear it as disagreement usually repeat themselves, and repetition is named explicitly in the descriptors as a coherence problem.

Three legitimate extensions, in order of value.

  1. Go down a level. Give the mechanism behind the claim you already made. Because the decision is made at the till, not at home — and that's where the price is visible.
  2. Give a case. A specific instance that the general claim predicts. Constructed examples are fine; textbook ones are not.
  3. Name the limit. Say where your claim stops holding. Though that only works where there's a cheap alternative available — otherwise you're just taxing poor people. This is the strongest of the three, because it demonstrates that you know the shape of your own argument.

What not to do. Restating the original claim in different words. The examiner asked precisely because the claim was already made; saying it again louder answers nothing and consumes the time you had to answer properly.

If you genuinely have no further reason, say so and reason forward out loud: That's a fair question — my instinct says yes, but now that I try to justify it I'm less sure, because… Hesitation of this kind is content related, which the Band 8 descriptor treats as acceptable rather than as a fault.
